newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, German above 97 deficit targets - Boissonnat.
newsitem.headline: France, German above 97 deficit targets - Boissonnat.

text.p: Ex-Bank of France council member Jean Boissonnat said in an article published on Sunday that France and Germany appeared to be overshooting public deficit targets for joining a single European currency, but said convergence was more important than exact figures.

Boissonnat said it was not absurd to estimate that the French public deficit in 1997 as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 was running closer to 3.5 percent than three percent but the fact this was also the case in Germany augured well for monetary union.

"If the Germans were at two percent and we were at four, the chances of convergence would be very weak. What matters is convergence between the main protagonists, more than than the exact figure," Boissonnat said in an article he contributed to the Journal de Dimanche.

"Without being able to put forward definite figures (there are eight months to run before the end of the year), it is not absurd to estimate that we, our neighbours and us, are closer to a deficit of around 3.5 percent than three percent for the current year," Boissonnat said.

He said while there was no doubting the political resolve of French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl to start monetary union on time, economic performance, especially deficits, would play a large part in which countries join.
"Now, actually, France and Germany - without which there would be no euro - are still overshooting the three percent (deficit) limit of gross domestic product," Boissonnat said.

Boissonnat said, however, that reducing the French deficit by half a percentage point of GDP was not an impossible feat even if painful financiallly and politically perilous. He said cutting the deficit/GDP ratio by that amount represented savings in the order of 40 billion francs.

Boissonnat also said the fact that tough policies may be needed to bring the deficit in line with the three percent target set out in the Maastricht Treaty was one justification for holding an early election in France.
"Whatever the measures to take may be, they will not be popular," Boissonnat said. "Better therefore to go ahead with elections before rather than after."
Speculation is rife in France that Chirac may call snap elections as soon as Monday.
